content.en: [The following is a version of a presentation that was made by Saheli at Ambedkar University, as part of the MA Gender Studies course module. The presentation started with the unmistakable 'He ji re', included video clips from performances of 'Kaun Jaat' and 'Mahaul Badalna Hai' and led to nearly three hours of wonderful discussions with students, questions and answers, and more songs!]

How does theatre form a text for the women's movement? Answering this question would require us to look at street plays in specific, and the ways in which street plays lend themselves to use in social movements, and the women's movement in particular. We talked briefly about some of the plays that we had used and had experiences of in Saheli, and then discussed the kind of issues they talk about, as well as the process of creating the plays and performing them actually tells us about the movements and the campaigns that they were a part of. These were 'Om Swaha', a play on dowry deaths that was part of the anti-dowry campaign of the 1980s, 'Norplant', a play on the dangers of contraceptives, part of  the health campaign, 'Mahaul Badalna Hai', a play about sexual harassment at the workplace designed to spread awareness about the Vishakha Guidelines, and 'Kaun Jaat', a play that was born out of the need to understand interconnections in the various axes of exploitation.

Street plays have long been a part of the folk culture in the Indian subcontinent, and been used by social movements in India as well to great effect. Typically loud, energetic and engaging performances given by actors, these plays seek to convey messages of critique and change in a simple way, through humour and songs. However, when it comes to the women's movement, street plays assume a greater significance. Firstly, street plays quite straightforwardly enable the aspect of accessing public space and bringing what is often considered to be private out into the public sphere, something feminist movements have always tried to do through various campaigns and issues. Most significantly, this can be seen in issues of violence against women, which has always been categorised as 'ghar ka maamla' or a private family issue, especially when ideas of shame and honour are invoked. The challenge has been to speak about it in public, in part to remove the stigma from the vich'm and also to enable the perpetrator to be punished, both in a social and legal sense.

'Om Swaha' was a play that belonged to the strong anti-dowry campaign of the 1980s, which took up the issue of dowry deaths and forced it into the public consciousness at a time when nobody was talking about dowry violence, when it was brushed away as a private matter. The campaign was widespread all over most of North India, as well as Maharashtra, with protests and demonstrations, all driven by the need to break the silence around dowry.

image.credit: Anti-dowry placards... a sign of those times

content.en: The play begins with the auctioning of young men, a comic scene to show the humiliation and harassment that women undergo when they are placed on the "marriage market". It then picks up the story of a young woman, starting from her birth to her marriage, and addressing the ill treatment she receives at the hands of her in-laws for failing to bring adequate dowry. Her parents refuse to take her back. For the last scene, the performers would break the fourth wall and ask the audience to choose between two versions of the last scene - the first, where the woman dies of violence in her husband's house or the second, where she stands up for her rights and ultimately leaves the house and is able to successfully get on with her life. Both versions would then be performed in order to bring out the pathos of the first scenario. The play was interspersed with Punjabi folk songs, in order to form a connection with the audience, as the locus of the anti-dowry movement was largely around Delhi, the site of highest instances of dowry related violence. However, the play was also translated and performed in many other parts of the country as well.

'Om Swaha' was performed over 300 times in the 1980's. It added to the urgency of the anti-dowry movement, as play performances became a way for women to speak out about the violence in their homes, and approach women groups for help. The play performed the dual purpose of not only bringing the issue into public dialogue, but also making the audience, and all of society by extension, responsible for ending the social evil of dowry.

Another significance of street plays we discussed was the effects of simply capturing a public place. Typically street plays are performed in marketplaces, on streets outside bastis or factories, on a busy lawn in a college, in a bustling street. Such places which are typically hostile to women, when playing host to a troupe of noisy, colourful women collecting an audience and performing for them, undergo a transformation - they become a space of dialogue, where women's issues are brought up into examination, where the possibility of change becomes real and shared. At the very least for the duration of the play's performance, the nature of public space itself becomes charged with a different kind of energy.

image.credit: The first ever performance of "Mahaul Badalna Hai"

content.en: Coming to the issues of women in the public space, the Supreme Court guidelines on the issue of sexual harassment at the workplace in 1997, which came to be known as the 'Vishakha guidelines', were the first of its kind in the country to define the ambit of sexual harassment faced by women, and marked the first time that the government acknowledged that workplaces could be hostile and discriminatory to women.

About a year after the guidelines came out, Saheli conducted a survey of women working in various fields of employment regarding their experiences in a hostile working environment and the kinds of harassment they faced. Following the survey, Saheli released a report in 1998, titled "Another Occupafional Hazard: Sexual Harassment at the Workplace". The findings of the survey pointed to three important things: first, the lack of recognition and trivialisation of the problem of sexual harassment at the workplace; second, the blaming of the victim for her own harassment; and third, the fact that while almost all women in all sectors experienced sexual harassment, the extent and nature of the violence was directly linked to their class, nature of the work, location of the work, level of job security, and so on. These were serious issues that needed to be addressed along with the need to spread awareness about the guidelines. Saheli had also worked on some cases of sexual harassment, which reinforced our feeling that we needed a concerted campaign. And so the idea of doing a street play was born.

The play 'Mahaul Badalna Hai' features 5 characters, all working women, who face differing degrees of harassment in their workplaces. An important device we evolved in the play is to not show the perpetrators of the harassment, as all too often, scenes of harassment become used for a voyeuristic and titillating effect, or if acted not too well, even hilarity! So, in effect, each scene simply has one side of a conversation - showing the woman going about her daily work, experiencing escalating provocation or attacks, and her reactions to it all, yet the presence of the harassers is all too ominous.

The larger issue of women's ownership of their bodies and their right not to be harassed is conveyed through two contrasting scenes. The first is a scene of victim blaming, where the woman who is complaining of being harassed is told it is her fault for wearing certain kinds of clothes, or overreacting to simple teasing, or even merely stepping out of the house to find work. The second, an ironic parallel, has a man whose wallet is stolen on the street and faces similar taunts from the onlookers; that it is the man's fault for having done something provocative to attract the attention of a thief. The irony emerging from the interplay of these two scenes then triggers a monologue directly to the audience on the absurdity and wrongness of blaming women for crimes against them.

The second scene provides an interesting instance of how humour is used in street plays. In that particular scene, the comic effect works to not overwhelm the audience with the doubts about the guidelines themselves. It keeps the play engaging, as it serves to show the absurdity of blaming the woman victim in a situation of sexual harassment. Humour is often used as a really good way to point out certain things that ought to strike us as obvious, and like with the "marriage auction" and the priest in 'Om Swaha', humour also takes on a sort of sinister tone, because it points out a significant issue in a lighthearted way, even as the audience is aware that the issue at hand is not trivial at all. The scene in "Mahaul Badalna Hai" for example conveys important things about how we look at bodily autonomy, and forces the audience to look at the uncomfortable fact of how easily we choose to ignore the question of bodily autonomy and ownership of one's own sexuality in the case of harassment.

Further, through the conversation amongst the characters, the play also tries to bring out the idea that consent has a very important role, as one does not want to take away the element of desire or playfulness in interactions between people.

"Mahaul Badalna Hai" is a play that has been performed since the early 2000's, by various groups and different casts at various times. Many of us have played multiple characters in the play at different times, with floating cast, all replaceable, people just come in and perform. Over the years, the songs, the discussions and the interactions that are part of a street play have become a good way for people to get involved in the women's movement. Some people even end up getting attached to their characters, and it's very interesting to see Sahelis across generations connecting over their shared experiences of the play! The play and its songs were written entirely by Saheli members, its episodes derived from actual narratives from the report. Today, the songs have become part of a larger women's movement songbook itself, contributing to how street plays are enmeshed within the movement as a whole.

image.credit: Performance of "Mahaul Badalna Hai" at Sultanpuri, Delhi, 2011

content.en: We also brought forth the point of change in reactions to the play from the audience over the years. In the early 2000's, the play was received with optimism that the proposed guidelines, the setting up of committees would lead to some advances in addressing sexual harassment at the workplace. However, audience discussions after play performances recently, in 2011-12 reveal a far greater cynicism with the workings of the law, especially as reports of threats, harassment and violence faced by women not only in their workplaces but other public spaces have become worryingly frequent. In such a milieu, in colleges especially, the talk has often turned into building solidarih'es with other women, through talking about their experiences and evolving strategies to help combat the everyday reality of sexual harassment.

The two other plays that we discussed had been part of very different kinds of campaigns. The street play titled 'Norplant' was developed and performed in 1991-92, as part of a sustained campaign against hazardous contraceptives, in particular Norplant. Introduced as part of the then government's family planning programme in the 1990's, Norplant was an alternative long acting hormonal contraceptive 'implant' that was surgically inserted in women's bodies. The campaign against Norplant was well underway, with mass protests, demonstrations and activists crashing press conferences by the time the play came about.

The campaign had an understanding of the connections that were being made between poverty and population explosion in the third world, which was driving a lot of the foreign funding behind contraceptive campaigns. Third world poor women became the easy targets of population control, and the play 'Norplant' came about with two main objectives - firstly to alert poor women, especially in urban bastis, to the trials and the contraceptive itself; and secondly to put pressure on the government to scrap the trials as they were hazardous and unethical.

According to a Saheli who was part of creating and performing the play, "The decision of a street play seemed the fastest way to get to the lower middle class and basti women before they became targets." The play sought to highlight the coercive family planning programme, the politics of multinational corporations and the role of the health ministry, by satirising key players such as ministers and doctors, renaming the Health Minister, Mr Fotedaar as Khotedaar, (meaning unreliable), recreating scenes of how decision makers make hasty decisions, take action that serves their only own/global/funding/election purposes, or simply for meeting 'population targets'. It is these very actions that adversely impact poor women who are the subjects of their trials, who are given wrong information to get their consent, and are ultimately refused medical action in the end when they need it.

The play was direct and satirical in its take on the Indian government, global governments and funding agencies. It was a well-travelled play that was performed in resettlement colonies and bastis all over the city, and always garnered a big audience of both men and women. The women in the audience were always responsive to the message, and shared their stories freely, leading to engaged discussions about reproductive health. Like 'Om Swaha', the cast included both men and women.

While all the plays mentioned above were quite clearly campaign devices, the story of 'Kaun Jaat' has been slightly different. One of the major issues Saheli and several women's groups in the country have engaged with is the problem of growing communalism and the influence of right wing forces in the country. Post Gujarat genocide in 2002, many troubling questions about women's roles in situations of communal conflict arose. There was a need to look at connections between caste identity, religious identity and so on, and examine the various ways in which women are socialised into these and how they negotiate them in everyday life, particularly in the context of marriage and the family. A study conducted by Saheli in this context involved interviewing women in Delhi from varying backgrounds, about their lives in the context of their various identities of caste, class, religion and sexuality. When the report, titled 'Talking Marriage, Caste and Community - Voices From Within' was complete, many discussions and presentations followed. But we felt that a play would be a good way to clarify these interconnections, and trigger debates on how they impact and define women's lives.

Hence, the play 'Kaun Jaat' (Literally, "What Caste?", but in common parlance, also used as "What regional, religious, linguistic and gender identity?"). Unlike the street play on sexual harassment, a script like Kaun Jaat would not primarily be a form of informationdissemination, but would rather be an awareness-raising exercise, an attempt to build connections between women's experiences and negotiations within the family, community and society. For us, Kaun Jaat became a way to articulate how women's differing locations in hierarchies shape the specificities of their oppressions, the challenges they face, and perhaps most importantly,to find ways to build bridges across these differences.

This was a challenging play to write and perform, since it dealt with a range of issues and did not focus on a single problem or resolufi'on. After much conversafi'on and playing around with ideas, we decided to use monologues, derived in part from the interviews we had done for the report. What was important here was to bring out the interconnections between different forms of exploitative systems, in such a way that it could shake the audience.

There were five monologues in all. The first character is a Dalit doctor, who talks about her experience of caste discrimination and the deep impact of the vicious anti-reservation movement in Delhi, especially within India's premium medical institution. Then there is a young Muslim woman who falls in love and marries a Hindu and abides by his family's condition to convert and subsume her own religious identity - her loneliness and pain is telling. The third is a woman who, years after being in a traditional arranged marriage who realises she is not quite 'happily married' like she was deluding herself. Then, a photographer talks about coming out as a lesbian to her family, even as she discusses the difficulty of working things out with her partner. The play's last monologue talks about sexual violence in situations of conflict - between communities and even with the State - and brings out the connections between different kinds of violence and oppressions, and how women's bodies are frequently the sites of violence. The monologues are interspersed with powerful poetry and satirical songs that show the absurdity of rigid religious and community norms that control women's lives.

The subtlety and irony with which Kaun Jaat plays, within the more direct parameters of a street play, has been received very differently in different contexts. While most audiences respond knowingly to the questions being raised, there have been some memorable instances where it has come across as reinforcing hierarchies, leading to audience members questioning the play and its message itself. All in all, Kaun Jaat has led to some very thoughtful and interesting discussions.

At the end of the presentation we once again raised the question as to why is it important for us to talk about street plays as a text for the women's movement. Street plays, both with their content and form, are important devices of individual campaigns or larger social questions that the women's movement seeks to undertake as we have seen above. The journey of a street play, from its conception to its writing to its performance, its discussions and its after life, can serve as an illustration of the life of the campaign and shed light on some facets of politics of the movement as a whole. In themselves, street plays are an important way of doing politics for the women's movement as well, in simple physical terms of gathering an audience that is mostly dominated by women, claiming a public space and turning it into a place of discussion and debate, and a creative way of reaching out to people, spreading awareness or raising concerns about issues. Street plays can thus provide us with an alternative history of the movement, embedded in the stories, reminiscences, discussions and songs that are associated with each play.The history of plays in a collective like Saheli is also one of reviving feminist energies, with new women joining in for the play performance but staying on for just about everything, and a language of protest and struggle embodied in songs and dialogues that link us across generations and groups.

content.credit: Performance of Kaun Jaat at Hyderabad Central University, 2010

content.en: The presentation took place before the students of the MA Gender Studies class, and there was an atmosphere of easy discussion wherein the audience was free to ask us questions and clarifications during our talk. After the presentation, the students had questions on many details of the campaigns and the process of writing plays, whether having a street play as a part of a campaign was seen as a kind of natural progression and so on. Us gregarious Sahelis ended up talking about movements and street plays and the stories of interactions that took place at various venues for a while longer, and we were even requested (quite persuasively!) to sing more songs, and so the day ended with the tune of
“Mashaale le kar chalna, ke ab tak raat baaki hai...”
